visual_features.color: dark brown to almost black coat, lighter greyish-brown underparts, pinkish bare rump patches
visual_features.body_shape: stocky tailless macaque with robust build
visual_features.distinctive_marks: no tail (stump only), prominent brow ridge, pink ischial callosities (buttock pads), heavy build
visual_features.pattern: uniform dark coat without contrasting markings

description: The Moor Macaque is a macaque species endemic to the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia. It is the only macaque species that naturally occurs in South Sulawesi. These primates are highly social, living in groups of 15–40 individuals with an adult sex ratio of 1 male to 0.5–2.7 females. They are diurnal and semi-terrestrial, spending much of their time in trees foraging and on the ground traveling. Their home range is typically 20–30 ha wide with a total daily travel distance of roughly 6.6 km. The population has declined dramatically from an estimated 56,000 in 1983 to under 10,000 in 1994 due to deforestation and habitat loss. They are sometimes called 'dog-ape' because of their dog-like muzzle, though they are Old World monkeys, not apes.
population_estimate: Estimated at under 10,000 mature individuals (down from ~56,000 in 1983). Density surveys found 6.3–63.2 individuals per km² in 1992. The population continues to decline due to habitat loss and fragmentation.
habitat: Moist deciduous forests up to 2,000 m above sea level, mosaics of forest with grasslands, areas of cultivation surrounded by primary and secondary forests, and karst (limestone) forest ecosystems. A large part of the remaining population is confined to karst tower forests in southwestern Sulawesi, where towers are 150–300 m tall with abundant fruit trees on top. They show significant ecological flexibility and can use several forest strata including secondary habitats.
threats: Habitat loss from agriculture and urban development
Deforestation of lowland forests over the past 50 years
Habitat fragmentation isolating populations and reducing genetic diversity
Human-wildlife conflict when macaques forage on crops
Surface mining operations affecting forest patches
Expanding human population encroaching on natural habitat
ecosystem_role: As frugivorous primates, Moor Macaques play a crucial role in seed dispersal and forest regeneration. They help support high densities of seedlings and saplings and facilitate gene flow among plant populations, which is vital for sustaining forest regeneration and restoring vegetation in degraded forests.
human_connection: Interactions between Moor Macaques and humans are becoming increasingly frequent in South Sulawesi due to habitat loss and human population growth. This often leads to conflict as they raid crops, but also creates opportunities for ecotourism and conservation education through projects like the Macaca Maura Project at Bantimurung-Bulusaraung National Park. The species was first described in Western science by Heinrich Rudolf Schinz in 1825.
what_students_can_do: Support conservation organizations working in Sulawesi like the Macaca Maura Project
Raise awareness about habitat conservation and deforestation in Indonesia
Study primatology and contribute to research on Sulawesi's endemic primates
Participate in ecotourism that supports local conservation efforts
Learn about sustainable agriculture practices to reduce habitat destruction
Understand the importance of karst forest ecosystems for biodiversity
fun_fact: Moor Macaques have a unique characteristic where almost every group contains an individual with mostly whitish fur, making groups easily identifiable
